name: Laura Flessel-Colovic
milestone_by_age_26: Won double gold (individual and team épée) at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics at age 25, the inaugural year for women's épée at the Olympics.
early_history_summary: Born in Guadeloupe, Flessel began fencing at age 7 after seeing Jean-François Lamour on television. She moved to Paris in 1990 at age 19 to train seriously, joining Racing Club de France. She won Pan American championships in 1991-92 and 1994, and took bronze at the 1995 World Championships before her Olympic breakthrough in 1996.
family_context_summary: Daughter of Edouard Flessel, a meteorologist, and Marie-Éva Flessel, a school teacher, in Pointe-à-Pitre, Guadeloupe. One of four children.
primary_early_advantage_tags: elite club training, early specialization, geographic relocation, dedicated coach
evidence_summary: Flessel-Colovic grew up in Guadeloupe and started fencing at age 7, inspired by a TV segment on Jean-François Lamour. She relocated to Paris at 19 to join Racing Club de France, an elite athletic organization, which gave her access to top-level coaching and competition. Her father was a meteorologist and mother a teacher — a middle-class background but no documented family-domain advantage in fencing. Her rapid rise from local competitions to Olympic double gold by 25 reflects exceptional physical talent, early specialization, and concentrated training in a fencing capital.
starting_point: Born to a middle-class family in Pointe-à-Pitre, Guadeloupe; father was a meteorologist, mother a school teacher.
current_position: Served as French Minister of Sports (2017-2018); retired from competitive fencing after 2012 Olympics; resides in France.

trajectory.event: Won bronze medal in individual épée at the World Championships in The Hague.
Won double gold (individual and team épée) at the Atlanta Olympics, the inaugural year for women's Olympic épée.
Won individual and team gold at the World Championships in La Chaux-de-Fonds.
Won individual bronze at the Sydney Olympics.
Won individual silver and team bronze at the Athens Olympics.
Carried the French flag at the London Olympics opening ceremony, her fifth and final Olympics.
Appointed French Minister of Sports by President Emmanuel Macron.

name: Daniel Buren
milestone_by_age_26: Began exhibiting in official competitions in 1964 at age 26, but his signature striped motif (1965, age 27) and the radical BMPT collective manifestations (1967, age 29) came after age 26; no material, independently verifiable artistic milestone by 26.
early_history_summary: Buren studied at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris and began exhibiting in official competitions in 1964. His iconic 8.7-cm vertical stripe motif was adopted in 1965, and the BMPT collective (with Mosset, Parmentier, Toroni) staged their first manifestation in January 1967.
evidence_summary: Buren attended the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris and began exhibiting in 1964 at age 26, but his defining artistic contributions — the striped visual tool (1965) and the BMPT collective actions (1967) — emerged after age 26. No material, independently verifiable milestone by 26 was found.

name: István Szabó
milestone_by_age_26: His thesis film Koncert (1963) won a prize at the International Short Film Festival Oberhausen at age 25, and he directed his first feature film The Age of Daydreaming in 1964 at age 25-26.
early_history_summary: Szabó was one of 11 admitted out of 800 applicants to the Academy of Drama and Film in Budapest, where he studied under Félix Máriássy. He directed several short films as a student, and his thesis film Koncert (1963) won a prize at Oberhausen. He was apprenticed to János Herskó at Hunnia Film Studio, enabling him to direct his first feature at 25 instead of spending a decade as an assistant.
family_context_summary: Son of a doctor from a long line of doctors in Budapest. The family were Jewish converts to Catholicism; his father died of diphtheria during the war when Szabó was a child.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a doctor; Szabó initially wanted to be a doctor too before being inspired by a book by Béla Balázs to pursue film. No direct family domain advantage in filmmaking.
primary_early_advantage_tags: elite film academy, mentor apprenticeship, wartime adversity, peer cohort
evidence_summary: Szabó was the son of a doctor from a long line of doctors in Budapest; his father died during WWII. He gained admission to the highly selective Academy of Drama and Film (11 of 800 accepted) and studied under Félix Máriássy, who became a father figure. His thesis film won a prize at Oberhausen at 25, and through apprenticeship to János Herskó at Hunnia Film Studio he directed his first feature at 25. His wartime childhood experiences and the 1956 Hungarian Revolution shaped his artistic vision.
starting_point: Born in Budapest to a doctor from a long line of doctors; Jewish family that had converted to Catholicism; father died of diphtheria during WWII when Szabó was a child.
current_position: Still active as a film director at age 88; resides in Budapest, Hungary. Academy Award winner for Mephisto (1981).

trajectory.event: Thesis film Koncert won a prize at the International Short Film Festival Oberhausen.
Directed first feature film The Age of Daydreaming, a Hungarian New Wave generation film.
Directed Father (Apa), which won the Golden Prize at the Moscow International Film Festival and Special Jury Prize at Locarno.
Mephisto won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film, his greatest international success.
Directed Sunshine, an epic spanning three generations of a Hungarian Jewish family.

name: Katja K
milestone_by_age_26: Her adult film career began in 1997 at age 29; no material milestone by age 26 was found. She was a university student before entering the adult industry.
early_history_summary: Born Sussi la Cour in Denmark, she studied experience leadership at Roskilde Universitetscenter before entering the adult film industry at age 29 in 1997. She starred in Zentropa-produced films and became a contract performer for SinCity in the US.
evidence_summary: Katja K (Sussi la Cour) studied at Roskilde University before entering the adult film industry at age 29 in 1997. Her fame came entirely after age 26, with no material milestone found before that age.

name: Michel Mayor
milestone_by_age_26: Completed a Master's in Physics (1966, age 24) and a Certificat d'Astronomie et d'Astrophysique (1968, age 26) from the University of Geneva; these are academic qualifications, not material career milestones. His Nobel Prize-winning exoplanet discovery came in 1995 at age 53.
early_history_summary: Mayor studied physics at the University of Lausanne, earning a Master's in 1966. He then moved to astrophysics at the University of Geneva, earning his astronomy certificate in 1968 and PhD in 1971. His early work focused on galactic dynamics and stellar kinematics.
family_context_summary: Born in Lausanne, Switzerland. Interested in science from age 10 but not specifically astronomy initially. No family background details documented.
evidence_summary: Mayor earned a Master's in physics (1966) and an astronomy certificate (1968) by age 26, but these are standard academic qualifications rather than material career milestones. His groundbreaking discovery of the first exoplanet orbiting a sun-like star (51 Pegasi b) came in 1995 at age 53, earning him the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics. No material milestone by 26 was found.

name: Raúl González
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic bronze with Spain at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics and silver at the 1996 European Championship, both at age 26.
early_history_summary: Born in Valladolid, Spain, González began playing handball at school in the early 1980s. He debuted in the top Spanish division in the 1989/90 season at age 19-20 with ADC Michelín (later BM Valladolid), and spent his entire 15-year playing career with the club. He earned over 50 international caps for Spain.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. From Valladolid, a handball-mad city in Spain.
primary_early_advantage_tags: early specialization, hometown club, domain immersion
evidence_summary: González grew up in Valladolid, a handball-mad city, and chose handball over football as a youth. He debuted in the top Spanish division at 19-20 and spent his entire career with his hometown club. No family background or financial advantage is documented. His path to Olympic bronze at 26 was built on sustained, early domain immersion and loyalty to one club.
starting_point: Born in Valladolid, Spain; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Head coach of the Serbia national handball team; previously coached Paris Saint-Germain and Vardar, winning the 2017 EHF Champions League.

trajectory.event: Debuted in the top Spanish handball division (Liga ASOBAL) with ADC Michelín.
Won Olympic bronze with Spain at Atlanta 1996 and silver at the European Championship in Spain.
Won the Copa ASOBAL with BM Valladolid, one of his best club-level memories.
Retired from playing and became assistant coach at BM Ciudad Real.
Won the EHF Champions League as head coach of RK Vardar.

name: Jenő Kamuti
milestone_by_age_26: Won World Team Champion in foil at the 1957 World Championships in Paris at age 20, and was a member of the Hungarian national foil team from 1956.
early_history_summary: Born in Budapest to a railway family, Kamuti joined BVSC at age 13 and was discovered by coach Nagy Árpád, then trained under Bay Béla after 1954. He won silver at the 1956 Junior World Championships and became World Team Champion in foil in 1957. He was also University World Champion in foil four times (1959, 1961, 1963, 1965) and individual World silver medalist in 1961 and 1963.
family_context_summary: Born into a railway family in Budapest; his father was a deputy director general of MÁV (Hungarian State Railways). One of the documented details is that he came from a vasutascsaládban (railway worker family).
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a MÁV deputy director general — a middle-class civil service position but no documented fencing domain advantage in the family.
primary_early_advantage_tags: elite club coaching, early specialization, national team pipeline, sustained mentorship
evidence_summary: Kamuti grew up in Budapest in a railway family (father was a MÁV deputy director general). He joined BVSC at 13 and was coached by Nagy Árpád and then Bay Béla, who provided sustained individualized training. He reached the Hungarian national foil team at 19 and won World Team gold at 20. His father's civil service position provided a middle-class background but no fencing-specific family advantage. His rapid rise was driven by early club-based specialization and high-quality coaching within the Hungarian fencing pipeline.
starting_point: Born in Budapest to a railway family; father was a deputy director general of Hungarian State Railways (MÁV).
current_position: President of the International Committee for Fair Play (CIFP) since 2000; retired surgeon and former fencer; resides in Hungary.

trajectory.event: Won silver at the Junior World Championships in Hamburg and joined the Hungarian national foil team.
Won World Team Champion in foil at the World Championships in Paris.
Won individual and team World silver medals in foil at the World Championships in Turin.
Won Olympic individual silver in foil at Mexico City.
Won second Olympic individual silver in foil at Munich.
Awarded the Pierre de Coubertin Trophy for his fair play career.
Elected President of the International Committee for Fair Play (CIFP).

name: Pete Conrad
milestone_by_age_26: Graduated from Princeton University with a BS in 1953 (age 23) and entered U.S. Navy flight training; by age 26 he was a naval aviator in training. No material, independently verifiable career milestone by 26. His astronaut selection came in 1962 (age 32) and first spaceflight in 1965 (age 35).
early_history_summary: Conrad graduated from Princeton University in 1953 and entered the U.S. Navy, becoming a naval aviator and then attending the Navy Test Pilot School at Patuxent River, Maryland. He served as a flight instructor and performance engineer before being selected as a NASA astronaut in September 1962.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Born in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.
evidence_summary: Conrad graduated from Princeton in 1953 at age 23 and entered Navy flight training. By 26 he was a naval aviator in training — a standard career path, not a material milestone. His astronaut selection (1962), first spaceflight (1965), and Apollo 12 moon landing (1969) all came well after age 26.

name: Albin Planinc
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Slovenian Chess Championship in 1968 at age 24, and achieved his first major international success by winning the Vidmar Memorial tournament in Ljubljana 1969 at age 25, finishing ahead of grandmasters including Svetozar Gligoric.
early_history_summary: Born in a working-class family in Briše, Slovenia, Planinc learned chess at age 7. He won the Slovenian youth championship in 1962 at age 18. While working assembling bicycles in a factory, he won the Vidmar Memorial in 1969 as a relatively unknown player, defeating established grandmasters. He was awarded the GM title in 1972.
family_context_summary: Born in a working-class family in Briše near Zagorje in German-occupied Slovenia. Worked in a bicycle factory while pursuing chess.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No family chess background mentioned.
primary_early_advantage_tags: working-class background, self-taught, factory worker, imaginative talent
evidence_summary: Planinc was born into a working-class family in rural Slovenia and learned chess at age 7. He won the Slovenian youth championship at 18 and the full Slovenian championship at 24, all while working in a bicycle factory. His stunning win at the 1969 Vidmar Memorial — ahead of grandmaster Gligoric and others — as an untitled factory worker demonstrated exceptional natural talent and self-driven chess development with no documented family advantages, coaching, or institutional support.
starting_point: Born in a working-class family in Briše near Zagorje, Slovenia (then German-occupied); no documented family advantages.
current_position: Died December 20, 2008 at age 64 in a mental institution in Ljubljana, Slovenia, after decades of severe depression.

trajectory.event: Won the Slovenian youth chess championship.
Won the full Slovenian Chess Championship.
Won the Vidmar Memorial tournament in Ljubljana, finishing ahead of grandmaster Gligoric and other titled players.
Awarded the Grandmaster title by FIDE.
Shared first place with Tigran Petrosian at the Amsterdam IBM tournament, ahead of Spassky and Kavalek.
Won team silver medal with Yugoslavia at the Chess Olympiad in Nice.
Died in a mental institution in Ljubljana after decades of severe depression.

name: Andy Bathgate
milestone_by_age_26: Named an NHL All-Star and finished 3rd in Hart Trophy (MVP) voting in 1956-57 at age 24 with 77 points; by 1957-58 at age 25 he was NHL First Team All-Star and Hart Trophy runner-up with 78 points.
early_history_summary: Born in Winnipeg, Bathgate joined the Guelph Biltmores of the OHA in 1949 as a 17-year-old. He began his NHL career with the New York Rangers in 1952-53, bouncing between the AHL/WHL and NHL before becoming a Rangers regular in 1954-55. He quickly became one of the NHL's top scorers, reaching 77 points by age 24.
primary_leverage_engine: Physical talent and early professional immersion
family_context_summary: Born in Winnipeg, Manitoba. His older brother Frank was also signed by the Rangers. Bathgate turned down university hockey scholarships to join the Guelph Biltmores junior system.
parent_family_domain_summary: Brother Frank Bathgate also played hockey and was signed by the Rangers first, creating a family pipeline to the organization. No parental domain advantage documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: junior hockey pipeline, sibling in sport, early NHL debut, Winnipeg hockey culture
evidence_summary: Bathgate grew up in Winnipeg, a hockey pipeline city for the Rangers. His older brother Frank was signed by the Rangers first, creating a family connection to the organization. Andy joined the Guelph Biltmores junior system at 17, turned down university scholarships, and reached the NHL by 20. He became a Rangers regular at 22 and was an NHL All-Star and Hart Trophy finalist by 24. His path was enabled by the Rangers' junior hockey pipeline and his brother's prior connection, though no significant family financial advantage is documented.
starting_point: Born in Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada; brother Frank also played hockey and was signed by the New York Rangers first.
current_position: Died February 26, 2016 at age 83 in Brampton, Ontario; final role was retired NHL great and Hockey Hall of Famer (inducted 1978).

trajectory.event: Became a regular with the New York Rangers in the 1954-55 NHL season.
Named NHL All-Star with 77 points; finished 3rd in Hart Trophy voting as league MVP.
Scored 40 goals (first Ranger to do so) and won the Hart Trophy as NHL MVP; named NHL First Team All-Star.
Tied Bobby Hull for the NHL scoring lead; named Rangers team captain.
Traded to Toronto Maple Leafs and helped them win the Stanley Cup.
Inducted into the Hockey Hall of Fame.
Died in Brampton, Ontario.

name: Karrie Webb
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1995 Women's British Open at age 20, becoming the youngest winner of the championship at the time. By age 21 she won her first LPGA tournament and set a rookie earnings record of over $1 million.
early_history_summary: Born in Ayr, Queensland, Australia, Webb started playing golf at age 8 with encouragement from her parents and maternal grandparents who all played. She teamed up with coach Kelvin Haller early in her career and had a distinguished amateur career representing Australia from 1992-1994, winning the Australian Amateur Stroke Play Championship in 1994. She turned professional in October 1994 at age 19.
family_context_summary: Parents and maternal grandparents all played golf and encouraged her early interest. Grew up in the small town of Ayr, Queensland. Started with plastic clubs at age 4 and received her first real set at age 8.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents and maternal grandparents all played golf, providing early domain exposure, equipment access, and encouragement from a young age.
primary_early_advantage_tags: family golf culture, early coaching, amateur career, domain immersion from childhood
evidence_summary: Webb grew up in Ayr, Queensland, in a family where both parents and maternal grandparents played golf, giving her early domain exposure from age 4. She started with coach Kelvin Haller early in her career and by her early teens was competing against top local male players. She represented Australia as an amateur (1992-94) and won the Australian Amateur Stroke Play in 1994. Turning pro at 19, she won the Women's British Open at 20. Her family's golf culture and sustained coaching from Haller were key early advantages, though the family was not documented as affluent.
starting_point: Born in Ayr, Queensland, Australia; parents and maternal grandparents all played golf, providing early domain exposure and encouragement.
current_position: Retired from full-time competitive golf; resides in Boynton Beach, Florida; 7-time major champion and World Golf Hall of Famer (inducted at age 25).

trajectory.event: Turned professional in October 1994 after winning the Australian Amateur Stroke Play Championship.
Won the Women's British Open, becoming the youngest champion in the event's history at the time.
Won first LPGA tournament (HealthSouth Inaugural) and set a rookie earnings record exceeding $1 million.
Named LPGA Player of the Year after winning six tournaments; qualified for World Golf Hall of Fame.
Became the youngest player (26) to win the LPGA Career Grand Slam; won 7 titles and Player of the Year again.
Won two more majors including the U.S. Women's Open, formally entering the Hall of Fame.

name: Lia Manoliu
milestone_by_age_26: Became the first Romanian woman to throw the discus over 40 meters (41.44 m) on 22 May 1950 at age 18, setting a national record. Competed at the 1952 Helsinki Olympics at age 20, finishing 6th.
early_history_summary: Born in Chișinău, Romania (now Moldova), Manoliu competed nationally in tennis, table tennis, volleyball, and basketball as a teenager before turning to throwing events at age 16. She quickly specialized in the discus, becoming the first Romanian woman over 40m at 18. She competed at six consecutive Olympics (1952-1972), winning gold in 1968.
family_context_summary: Born in Chișinău, Kingdom of Romania (now Moldova). Multi-sport athlete from a young age. Graduated from the Polytechnic Institute of Bucharest in the mid-1950s.
primary_early_advantage_tags: multi-sport background, natural throwing ability, early national record
evidence_summary: Manoliu was born in Chișinău and excelled in multiple sports as a teenager before specializing in discus at 16. By 18 she set a Romanian national record as the first woman over 40m. No family background, financial advantage, or coaching details are documented in reviewed sources. Her early milestone was driven by natural athletic ability across multiple sports and early specialization in throwing events within the Romanian sports system.
starting_point: Born in Chișinău, Kingdom of Romania (now Moldova); family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Died January 9, 1998 at age 65 in Bucharest; final role was President of the Romanian Olympic Committee (1990-1998).

trajectory.event: Became the first Romanian woman to throw the discus over 40 meters (41.44 m), setting a national record.
Competed at her first Olympics in Helsinki, finishing 6th in the discus; was Romanian national champion.
Won Olympic bronze medal in the discus at the Rome Olympics.
Won second Olympic bronze medal in the discus at the Tokyo Olympics.
Won Olympic gold medal in the discus at Mexico City on her first throw, an Olympic record.
Became the first track and field athlete to compete at six consecutive Olympics, finishing 9th in Munich.
Elected President of the Romanian Olympic Committee.
Died in Bucharest.
